about: What every kind of object in a Kerbside world is made of, how it is moved past, and how it breaks. Three layers: a material (what steel or turf is like), an archetype (what a street light or a tree generally is), and the instance the renderer draws (its place, its geometry and its basis: measured, mapped or inferred). Numbers here are archetype estimates from typical published values, never a measurement of a particular object; an instance's own basis is reported beside them and never relaxes its collision.

player.notes: One radius for both: within interaction_radius_m of the player the objects are described (Nearby) and are solid to the player. Anything whose top is within step_height_m of the feet is stepped over; anything whose bottom is head_clearance_m or more above the feet is walked under; between the two, the archetype's traversal decides.

traversal.walk_on: It is the ground underfoot: stood and walked on.
traversal.step_over: Low enough to step over without breaking stride.
traversal.climb_over: Too high to step over; climbed or vaulted where a game allows it, otherwise gone around.
traversal.go_around: Solid at body height: the player goes around it.
traversal.walk_under: Overhead: walked under while its bottom clears the head.
traversal.pass_through: Soft: walked through, and may slow the player.
traversal.enter: Solid outside; entered only through its door.

collision_sources.ground: Part of the walkable ground: the ground-height code stands the player on it.
collision_sources.footprint: A building: its footprint and walls stop the player, and its door lets them in.
collision_sources.mesh: The drawn mesh itself: the part of it between step height and head clearance is solid.
collision_sources.explicit: Colliders the layer registers itself (fallen logs and stumps, tunnel walls, doors).
collision_sources.host: Mounted on something else that does the stopping: a window or trim in its wall, a picture on its wall.

durability_levels.0: Static: solid, never damaged. Distant scenery and the ground.
durability_levels.2: Physical breakage: impact energy, failure mode and debris.
durability_levels.3: Structural simulation: reserved for specialist games.

rules: Collision and traversal come from the archetype and the geometry, never from the basis: an inferred tree is as solid as a surveyed one, and stays labelled inferred.

break_energy_j is the impact energy at which the archetype is expected to fail at its typical size; break_scales_with says what it grows with. A game that enables destruction may scale it; nothing here is a measured breaking force.
Friction is a shoe-on-surface coefficient (static, dynamic, wet); Unreal's physical material takes static and dynamic, the wet value is for weather.
Whether an object may actually be broken, opened or moved is an experience rule: the catalogue says what an archetype supports, a game says what it allows.

optics is how a material meets light: roughness (0 a mirror, 1 chalk), specular (the share mirrored head on, from its refractive index or the bare metal), albedo (the share of visible light, 400-700 nm, scattered back: grass and asphalt about a tenth, concrete a third) and albedo_range (what examples of it on a street span; a painted material's is as wide as paint's, black to white). A drawn surface outside its range is tinted into it. Published values for the material as it stands on a street, not measurements of these objects.

surfaces.notes: A name is looked up with any '|' suffix dropped and its first space read as ':' (the renderer writes both 'furniture street_light' and 'furniture:street_light'); a post named after its fence ('fence:chainlink_post') is that fence. An exact name wins, then the longest matching prefix. 'ground:*' and 'furniture:*' left over are small mapped objects the page drew without a kind of their own: they are solid at body height, as a bollard is.

mechanics.about: How each material meets force: strength, hardness, toughness and stiffness from published tables (each substance lists its sources), and how a contact between two things plays out from those figures and the shapes that meet (docs/city/mechanics.mjs, docs/62-material-mechanics.md). A catalogue material names its substance in its own 'mechanics' field; finer substances (wood species, blade steels, tissue) are for held things and particular objects.
mechanics.units: SI in the field names: MPa, GPa, J/m2 (fracture energy), MPa m^0.5 (fracture toughness), HV (Vickers number: MPa = 9.807 HV), N (Janka side hardness: the force to sink an 11.28 mm ball half its diameter, so its pressure in MPa is the force / 100), kg/m3, metres. Wood strengths are along the grain unless named perpendicular.

sources.usda_wood_handbook: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (FPL-GTR-190, 2010), Table 5-3a/5-3b: specific gravity, MOE, MOR, compression parallel and perpendicular, shear, tension perpendicular and side (Janka) hardness, green and at 12% moisture
sources.wood_elastic_ratios: Wood Handbook ch. 5, Table 5-1: E_T/E_L about 0.04-0.08 and E_R/E_L about 0.07-0.11; an across-the-grain modulus of E_L/16 is used
sources.wood_fracture: Jeronimidis 1980 (Proc. R. Soc. B 208:447): work of fracture across the grain about 10^4 J/m2; Stanzl-Tschegg et al. 1995 (Wood Sci. Technol. 29:31) and Patton-Mallory & Cramer 1987: splitting along the grain 100-600 J/m2; both scaled here by specific gravity to the 1.5 power (Ashby, Gibson et al. 1985)
sources.nds_withdrawal: American Wood Council, National Design Specification (2018) 12.2.3: nail withdrawal W = 1380 G^2.5 D lb per inch of penetration (the residual grip of displaced wood on a steel shank)
sources.felling: Felling practice: a hinge of about a tenth of the diameter holds a tree until it tips (USDA Forest Service Saw Program; Dent, Professional Timber Falling 1974); trees are built with a bending safety factor of about 4 against storms (Mattheck 1994)
sources.asm_metals: ASM Handbook vol. 1-2 and MatWeb typical values: A36/1018 steel (yield 250 MPa, UTS 400-440, 120-130 HV, K_IC above 100 MPa m^0.5), 6061-T6 (276/310 MPa, 107 HV, K_IC 29), grey iron (UTS 200 MPa, 210 HV, K_IC 18), annealed copper (70/220 MPa, 50 HV)
sources.blade_steels: Hardened blade steels: X50CrMoV15/440C at HRC 56-58 (610-650 HV, yield about 1.8 GPa, K_IC 20-25 MPa m^0.5) and plain carbon axe steel at HRC 50-54 (510-560 HV, K_IC 40-50); Verhoeven, Steel Metallurgy for the Non-Metallurgist (ASM 2007); Landes 2006 (knife edge retention)
sources.glass: Soda-lime float glass: E 72 GPa, 550 HV, K_IC 0.75 MPa m^0.5 (Varshneya, Fundamentals of Inorganic Glasses 2006); characteristic bending strength 45 MPa for large areas (EN 572-1) and about 120 MPa for small highly stressed areas under short loads (Haldimann, Luible & Overend, Structural Use of Glass 2008); fully tempered surface compression 69-150 MPa (ASTM C1048, EN 12150) in a layer about a fifth of the thickness deep
sources.ceramics: Y-TZP zirconia (1250 HV, K_IC 6-10, flexural 900-1200 MPa) and WC-Co carbide (1500-1700 HV, K_IC 10-12, flexural 2000+ MPa); Munz & Fett, Ceramics (Springer 1999); glazed stoneware after Ashby
sources.rock: Granite (E 50-70 GPa, UCS 130-250 MPa, tensile 7-25, K_IC 1-2.5) and sandstone (E 10-30, UCS 20-170, tensile 2-8, K_IC 0.3-1.2): Goodman, Introduction to Rock Mechanics (1989); Jaeger, Cook & Zimmerman (2007); Atkinson 1984 (fracture toughness)
sources.concrete_masonry: Concrete: f'c 25-40 MPa, tensile about 10% of that, E 25-35 GPa, fracture energy 75-150 N/m (ACI 318; fib Model Code 2010); clay brick: compressive 20-60 MPa, E 10-20 GPa (Hendry, Structural Masonry); quartz aggregate about 1100 HV
sources.ice: Petrovic 2003 (J. Mater. Sci. 38:1): ice E 9-10 GPa, K_IC 0.05-0.15 MPa m^0.5, tensile 0.7-3.1 MPa, compressive 5-25 MPa; indentation hardness 30-100 MPa between 0 and -20 C (Barnes, Tabor & Walker 1971, Proc. R. Soc. A 324:127)
sources.tissue: Skin: tensile 17-28 MPa at failure strains of 0.3-0.7 and tangent modulus 50-100 MPa (Annaidh et al. 2012, J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater. 5:139); cutting toughness 1.5-5 kJ/m2 (Pereira et al. 1997; Shergold & Fleck 2004, Proc. R. Soc. A 460:3037); fat and muscle moduli 1-100 kPa (McKee et al. 2011); meat toughness 1-4 kJ/m2 (Purslow 1985)
sources.bone: Cortical bone: E 15-20 GPa, UTS 100-150 MPa, compressive 170-200, K_IC 2-6 MPa m^0.5, hardness 0.4-0.7 GPa (Currey, Bones 2002; Zioupos & Currey 1998)
sources.food: Apple and potato flesh: moduli 2-6 MPa, failure strains 0.1-0.25, fracture toughness 100-300 J/m2 (Vincent 1990; Khan & Vincent 1993, J. Texture Stud. 24:423)
sources.polymers: Ashby, Materials Selection in Mechanical Design (4th ed. 2011) property data: polypropylene, polycarbonate, LDPE film, natural and filled rubbers; tearing energy of filled rubber 10-50 kJ/m2 (Rivlin & Thomas 1953; Gent 2001)
sources.sheets: Cotton duck canvas tensile 30-60 MPa, failure strain about 0.15, cutting toughness 2-5 kJ/m2; paper 30-80 MPa at strain 0.02-0.05, tearing energy 2-10 kJ/m2 (Niskanen, Paper Physics 2012); corrugated board after the same
sources.soils: Soil cone index 0.5-3 MPa moist loam, under 1 MPa for turf and sand (ASAE S313; Bengough & Mullins 1990); soil moduli 5-50 MPa
sources.friction_pavement: Rubber on pavement: dry 0.7-0.9, wet 0.4-0.6 (FHWA, Guide for Pavement Friction 2009); rubber on wet smooth glass 0.1-0.3; rubber on ice 0.1-0.2 cold and 0.02-0.07 near melting (Persson 2000, Sliding Friction; Hayhoe & Shapley 1989)
sources.friction_skin: Skin friction on smooth and rough surfaces 0.3-1.5, rising with adhesion on smooth surfaces and falling once wet (Derler & Gerhardt 2012, Tribol. Lett. 45:1); chalk dries sweat and raises friction on rock (Amca et al. 2012, J. Sports Sci. 30:669)
sources.friction_climbing: Sticky climbing rubber on dry granite and sandstone about 0.9-1.3; slab (friction) climbing in such rubber to about 40-45 degrees on dry rock
sources.finger_strength: Maximum two-handed hang force on a 20-23 mm edge: about 0.5-0.65 body weight for non-climbers, 0.9-1.1 for intermediate and 1.3-1.6 for elite climbers; the force falls with edge depth roughly as its square root (Baláš et al. 2012, Eur. J. Sport Sci. 12:16; Amca et al. 2012; Bourne et al. 2011)
sources.gecko: Hawkes et al. 2015 (J. R. Soc. Interface 12:20140675): gecko-type dry adhesive tiles of about 140 cm2 a hand let a 70 kg person climb vertical glass; such adhesives need smooth surfaces
sources.stab: Stab energies 20-115 J, with body-armour test energies of 24, 33 and 43 J (Horsfall et al. 1999; HOSDB Body Armour Standard 2007); a sharp knife point pierces skin at about 10-50 N (Knight 1975; O'Callaghan et al. 1999, Int. J. Legal Med. 112:236; Ankersen et al. 1999)
sources.edge_radius: Edge radii: razor blades 0.1-0.3 µm, sharp kitchen knives 0.3-1 µm, dull 2-10 µm; cutting force rising about linearly with edge radius in soft solids (McCarthy et al. 2007, J. Mater. Process. Technol. 189:25; Schuldt et al. 2016)
sources.cutting: Atkins 2009, The Science and Engineering of Cutting: cutting force per unit length = fracture toughness + bluntness + wedge (plastic) + friction terms; slicing lowers the push force by about 1/(1+xi^2)^0.5 for a slice/push ratio xi
sources.indentation: Johnson 1985, Contact Mechanics: Hertz contact, yield at a mean pressure about 1.1 Y, fully plastic at the hardness (about 3 Y); Lawn, Evans & Marshall 1980 (J. Am. Ceram. Soc. 63:574): radial crack length c from K_IC = chi P / c^1.5, chi = 0.016 (E/H)^0.5
sources.plates: Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain (8th ed.), Table 11.2: circular plates under central load and the equivalent contact radius r' = (1.6 r^2 + t^2)^0.5 - 0.675 t; point impedance of a thin plate Z = 8 (D rho h)^0.5 (Cremer & Heckl, Structure-Borne Sound)
sources.tool_geometry: Tool geometry: chef's knives about 15-20 degrees a side at the edge on a flat grind 2-2.5 mm thick, tip radius 0.1-0.5 mm (forensic measurements: O'Callaghan et al. 1999); felling axe bits about 25-30 degrees at the edge and 20-25 mm thick 80-90 mm back; splitting mauls 35-45 degrees; swing energies from rules.json tools
sources.soil_cutting: McKyes 1985, Soil Cutting and Tillage (Elsevier), ch. 2-4, and Reece 1964 (Proc. Instn Mech. Engrs 179): a blade's draft F = w (gamma d^2 N_gamma + c d N_c + c_a d N_ca); typical cohesion 0-5 kPa for sand and duff, 10-20 kPa for moist loam, friction angles 25-42 degrees, soil-metal friction about two thirds of the internal angle; Terzaghi bearing factors N_q = e^(pi tan phi) tan^2(45 + phi/2); root cohesion 5-20 kPa in turf (Wu 1979; Gray & Sotir 1996)
sources.push_strength: Snook & Ciriello 1991 (Ergonomics 34:1197) and Chaffin, Andersson & Martin, Occupational Biomechanics: a standing adult's initial horizontal push about 300-500 N with good footing (sustained about 60% of it); a push is also capped by the shoes' friction on the ground times body weight; rolling resistance 0.010-0.015 for car tyres on asphalt (Gillespie, Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics), 0.02-0.04 for small hard casters
sources.balance: Hof, Gazendam & Sinke 2005 (J. Biomech. 38:1): the extrapolated centre of mass x + v sqrt(l/g) must stay within the base of support; a single recovery step handles about 1-1.5 m/s (Hsiao & Robinovitch 1999), beyond which a pushed person falls
sources.nail_driving: Euler buckling of a fixed-pinned column P = pi^2 E I / (0.7 L)^2 and the plastic moment of a round section M_p = sigma_y d^3 / 6 (Gere & Timoshenko, Mechanics of Materials), for the exposed length of a nail; common nail heads and lengths from ASTM F1667 (16d: 3.3 mm shank, 7.1 mm head, 89 mm long)
sources.coating_films: Wicks, Jones, Pappas & Wicks, Organic Coatings: Science and Technology, 4th ed. (Wiley 2017), ch. 4 (mechanical properties of films) and ch. 24-25 (architectural and automotive coatings): exterior acrylic latex films sit near or below their glass transition at room temperature (tensile 2-8 MPa, elongation 100-400 %, modulus 0.05-0.5 GPa); crosslinked alkyd and polyester enamels are glassy (modulus 1-4 GPa, tensile 20-50 MPa, elongation 2-10 %); free-film tensile figures by ASTM D2370
sources.clearcoat_nanoindentation: Automotive two-pack acrylic-urethane clearcoats by nanoindentation and scratch: modulus 3-5 GPa, hardness 0.15-0.3 GPa, cracking under a scratch tip at 3-5 % strain (Lin, Blackman & Matheson, Prog. Org. Coat. 40 (2000) 85-91; Jardret, Lucas, Oliver-Leblond & Oliver, J. Adhesion 2000)
sources.coating_adhesion: Pull-off adhesion by ASTM D4541 / ISO 4624: architectural latex over render and masonry 1-2 MPa (it parts in the render's own skin), alkyd over primed wood 2-4 MPa, polyester powder over pretreated steel and aluminium 8-15 MPa, an OEM car paint stack over its e-coat above 10 MPa; the pull-off figure is taken as the interface's shear strength too (shear adhesion runs at 1-2 times it)
sources.coating_thickness: Dry film thickness (ASTM D7091 gauges): two coats of exterior latex 75-100 um (about 40-50 um a coat), an alkyd primer and two gloss coats 100-120 um, a powder coat 60-80 um, an OEM car stack about 100 um (e-coat 20, primer 30, base 15, clear 40-50); hot thermoplastic road marking 3 mm
sources.scratch_hardness: Scratch hardness HSp = 8 P / (pi w^2), the load over the front half of the groove's circle (ASTM G171; Bowden & Tabor, The Friction and Lubrication of Solids, 1950): a sliding sphere bears only on its leading half, so its groove is the depth at which half its plastic contact carries the load
sources.scratch_ratio: One solid scratches another only if it is about 20 % harder than it (Tabor, 'Mohs's hardness scale: a physical interpretation', Proc. Phys. Soc. B 67 (1954) 249); for a gritty composite (render, concrete, brick) what must be out-hardened is its grit, not its binder
sources.representative_strain: Tabor's representative strain under a spherical indenter, e = 0.2 a / R (Tabor, The Hardness of Metals, 1951; Johnson, Contact Mechanics, 1985, s. 6.2): the strain a coat carried down with a dent is stretched to
sources.confined_layer: A thin plastic layer squeezed under a flat with sticking friction bears p = Y (1 + 2 a / (3 sqrt 3 t)), the slab solution for upsetting (Johnson & Mellor, Engineering Plasticity, 1973, ch. 11): a film thinner than its contact is held in by the faces either side and does not flow first
sources.shear_lag: A cracked brittle film on a substrate lifts off over the length its own stress can be carried by the interface: crack spacing lambda = pi sigma_f t / tau (Agrawal & Raj, Acta Metall. 37 (1989) 1265), so a flake runs half that either side of the crack
sources.gypsum_board: ASTM C1396: 1/2 in gypsum board must carry 107 lbf (476 N) at mid-span over 14 in on a 12 in wide sample (bearing edges parallel), a flexural stress of about 5 MPa for the paper-faced board -- three times its bare core's
sources.beams: Section strength and stiffness (Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Tables 8.1 and 11.2): a beam on two supports loaded at mid-span F = 4 M / L, k = 48 E I / L^3; a post fixed at its foot and struck at a height F = M / L, k = 3 E I / L^3; elastic M = sigma Z (Z = b h^2 / 6, pi d^3 / 32, pi (D^4 - d^4) / (32 D)), fully plastic M = sigma_y Z_p (Z_p = b h^2 / 4, d^3 / 6, (D^3 - d^3) / 6); a plate under a central load sigma = 3 F / (2 pi t^2) ((1 + nu) ln(a / r0) + 1)

alkyd_enamel.name: Alkyd gloss enamel film (doors, trim, furniture, railings)

powder_coat.name: Polyester powder coat (poles, racks, cabinets, metal panels)

auto_clearcoat.name: Car paint: two-pack clearcoat over base, primer and e-coat

coatings.about: A coat is a layer of its own over what it covers: its own substance (hardness, stiffness, failure strain), its own thickness, and what holds it on (adhesion, the interface's strength). A scratch in it stays in it until it is cut through; what is under is marked only by what out-hardens that too.

exterior_latex.name: Two coats of exterior acrylic latex

alkyd_enamel.name: Alkyd primer and two gloss coats

cladding_coats.about: The coat each wall cladding class (claddings.classes) wears: painted classes the paint the house's colour is in; brick, stone, tile and vinyl show their own colour and have none.

forms.about: The shape each archetype meets a blow or a push with: shape (box: panels round a frame; beam: on two supports; post: fixed at its foot; panel: a plate held at its edges; round: a log lying; wall and ground: fixed, a half-space at the scale of a contact), its section (b_m x h_m, or d_m and a tube's wall_m), its span_m, the radius of its corners and edges (edge_r_m), its biggest face (face_m2), its coat, its own mass (mass_kg) where it is one thing, and the bending strength of a made board where it is not its substance's (flexural_mpa). Archetypes not listed are fixed half-spaces of their material with no coat.

contactors.about: What touches a surface when something is held, stood on or climbed: its adhesive share (sticks by true contact area, so best on smooth clean surfaces), its hysteresis share (grips by deforming over the surface's texture, so best on rough ones), a base share (boundary and ploughing friction), how much water it holds (sweat), and any dry adhesive (gecko tiles: a shear stress over its area that needs a smooth surface). Calibrated against the catalogue's shoe friction and the published ranges in sources.

steel.name: Bare steel (a blade or a tool face sliding on what it strikes)

implements.about: The geometry and make of what strikes: an edge (its thickness at each distance back from the apex, the length that meets the work), a tip (width and thickness at each distance from the point, how many sharp sides), a face (its curvature and size), and the strike mass. Radii are the state of a new tool; the engine returns them worn. Each names its substance.
